messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Luke is a 28-year-old social media manager who lives with his girlfriend in a mid-sized city. He spent eighteen months in Afghanistan as part of a convoy security unit. What happened one afternoon near a dried riverbed is something he can recount only in pieces—there was an explosion, a vehicle ahead of him lifted and fell, and then he saw the driver’s leg. The memory does not come as a continuous story. Instead, he feels a sudden wash of heat and nausea, his heart slamming, without any clear picture attached. Other times a fragment surfaces: the sound of the rotor blades from the medevac helicopter, the way the dust swirled, the sight of a boot that was still laced. He knows the event happened—he was there—but the whole thing can feel so extreme that he sometimes has to tell himself it really did occur.

When Luke returned home, he threw himself back into his civilian job, managing brand accounts and scheduling posts for a regional outdoor gear company. The work itself is safe, but the visual environment is not. He scrolls through user-generated content and sometimes comes across a photo of a hiker with a bloody gash on their leg from a fall. The image hooks him: his throat tightens, his palms sweat, and he has to look away fast. He has learned to flag such content without really looking. His girlfriend, Jen, had asked him to drive them to a weekend getaway a few months ago, and he felt his chest seize. Being in the car with her, the passenger seat that should be empty, the road ahead—it triggered a physical reactivity he could not talk through. He muttered that he was tired and asked her to drive instead. Now she always drives when they go out together, and he knows she wonders why, but he cannot explain it without sounding broken.

Avoidance has become a kind of invisible architecture in his life. He never walks past a military recruiting office or a police car if he can help it. If one passes him on the street, he turns away or crosses a block early. He has stopped going to the gym entirely because any sensation of his body under strain—muscles burning, breathing hard—makes him feel as if he is back in that moment of adrenalized survival. Before any conversation with a coworker or even with Jen, he runs through what he might say, over and over, to make sure nothing catches him off guard, because spontaneity feels dangerous. At night, he lies in bed with his back to the door, his ears tuned for the sound of a helicopter overhead—rare, but when it happens, he is instantly, rigidly awake. Jen has accidentally touched his shoulder from behind twice in the past month, and both times he flinched violently, nearly knocking over a glass. She says she feels like she has to give him a warning before she comes near him.

What frightens Luke most is the conviction that he has permanently changed for the worse. He looks at his coworkers and his girlfriend, people who have not been through what he has, and he believes he is now a different species. Somebody else, he tells himself, would not have let the situation happen in the first place—would have seen the threat, made a different call, not been where that IED was waiting. He has come to feel like an outsider in every ordinary setting, watching from the other side of a glass wall. His relationship with Jen has grown quieter; he knows she senses the distance, but he cannot bridge it.

He finally sought help after a week when he rehearsed every single conversation at work and still felt flattened by a nausea that came without warning. The helicopter sound had passed overhead three nights in a row, and he had not slept. More than anything, he wants to feel as if he belongs in his own life again, but he is terrified that the damage is already done.
